title: Relief rally. Not a policy reset.
deck: My read after Monday's close: less pressure from oil and longer-term yields is welcome, but it does not erase last week's Fed tightening. Separate improving valuation conditions from evidence that a company's future cash flows have actually improved.

sections.title: The relief was further out on the curve.
sections.body: Treasury's official daily observations put the two-year yield at 4.76%, unchanged from Friday, while the ten-year fell from 5.01% to 4.96% and the thirty-year from 5.34% to 5.29%. The 10Y–2Y spread narrowed from 25 to 20 basis points. My interpretation: longer-duration borrowing conditions eased, but this was not a uniform repricing of the curve toward cheaper money. Nominal yields alone cannot separate inflation expectations, real rates and term premium. These are consistent daily par-yield observations, not executable bond quotes or an intraday event study.

sections.title: A strong index day is not a breadth measure.
sections.body: AP's Monday closes were S&P 500 7,764.70 (+1.5%), Dow 52,048.83 (+0.7%) and Nasdaq Composite 27,122.09 (+2.3%); the Russell 2000 gained 0.5%. Percentage changes are rounded. My inference: the gap between benchmarks argues against treating the session as equal relief for every business. An index return does not reveal the proportion of advancing shares, earnings revisions or the financing conditions facing smaller borrowers. The bullish counterargument is that lower discount rates can legitimately lift long-lived cash flows even without an immediate earnings upgrade. That is a valuation mechanism, not proof that those cash flows will arrive.

sections.title: Cheaper oil helps, if the improvement lasts.
sections.body: AP reported Brent down 3.4% to $100.34 per barrel and described continuing constraints on Middle Eastern oil shipments. My assessment: a sustained supply improvement could ease costs for transport and other energy users, but one day's commodity move is insufficient reason to rebuild a multi-year margin forecast. Hedges, inventories and contracts delay transmission; competition may pass savings to customers rather than shareholders. For producers, the same price decline can reduce revenue. The countercase is a temporary easing of geopolitical risk that reverses before operating costs change. Watch physical supply and company commentary, not just optimistic headlines.

sections.title: Keep the policy rate and the valuation assumptions separate.
sections.body: On 16 September, the Fed raised its target range by 25 basis points to 3.75–4.00%. Its projections put the median year-end policy-rate midpoint at 4.1% for both 2026 and 2027; these are conditional participant judgments, not promises. The same projections put 2026 real GDP growth at 2.3%, measured fourth-quarter to fourth-quarter. My interpretation: tighter policy and continued growth can coexist, so neither a blanket earnings downgrade nor an automatic return to cheap financing follows. In the DCF, test discount-rate relief with cash flows unchanged, then test operating improvements separately. Combining both immediately can double-count an optimistic narrative without independent evidence for either assumption.

watch: Would lower longer-term yields persist without a deterioration in growth expectations? Falling yields alongside weaker company demand would change the interpretation.
Look for sustained oil-supply improvements and evidence of lower input costs reaching margins. A renewed supply disruption would weaken the relief thesis.
Check whether gains broaden beyond the strongest benchmark and whether company guidance supports the cash flows assumed in valuations. Index strength alone cannot answer either question.
caveat: Codex's analysis, not Owen's personal view or investment advice. Equities and the oil report cover the completed 21 September US session. Treasury values are official 21 September daily par yields, compared with 18 September; they can differ from news reports' market quotes. Fed policy and projections were released 16 September. Research cutoff is shown in EDT (UTC−4) and HKT (UTC+8). This is dated research, not live commentary. Interpretations are conditional, causal links are not established by simultaneous price moves, and projections are not realized outcomes.
